outcomes.original: Filing step: Form LLC or corporation with California Secretary of State and obtain federal EIN. What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) online at bizfile.sos.ca.gov. Within 90 days, file the Statement of Information ($20 LLC, $25 corporation). Apply for an Employer Identification Number (EIN) at irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/apply-for-an-employer-identification-number-ein-online the same day; it is issued immediately and free. The entity name and EIN are required for the business registration, bank account, lease, and all city permits.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector and file fictitious business name (DBA) with the County Clerk. What to say: Register online at sftreasurer.org/business within 30 days of starting business; the fee is tiered by gross receipts ($55–$95 for most new restaurants, plus $4 state fee). You will receive a Business Account Number (BAN) required by every other city department. If your public-facing name differs from the legal entity name, file a fictitious business name statement with the County Clerk in person or by mail ($60–$120), then publish once a week for four weeks in an approved newspaper and file proof of publication within 45 days. Banks and other agencies will ask for the filed FBN statement.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Hire an architect to prepare building permit plans for tenant improvements, kitchen, and change of use. What to say: Engage a San Francisco restaurant architect to prepare stamped plans for the commercial kitchen hood, finishes, equipment layout, ADA upgrades, and any structural or MEP changes. Submit DPH health plan check and DBI building permit applications at the same time so both departments review in parallel. The building permit application must show the existing and proposed occupancy groups and occupant load; the architect will determine these from code and the layout. Make sure the DBI routing includes Planning (automatic under PC Section 175), Health, Fire, Public Works (for grease interceptor), and any other agencies. Budget 21–60 days for DPH plan review and 14–120 days for building permit review and inspections.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Submit DPH health plan check application with menu, equipment list, and scaled drawings. What to say: Apply online at sfdph.org/dph/EH/Food with your BAN, EIN, and a federal tax ID. Include two sets of scaled plans showing equipment placement, finishes, hand sinks, prep areas, storage, and the menu describing preparation methods. DPH will assign a plan reviewer; schedule a pre-final inspection at ~80% completion and a final inspection at least two weeks before your target opening. The flat fee for a new restaurant is $2,207 (8 hours) as of FY 2026–27, with additional review at $276/hour. Approval is required before DBI will issue the building permit final.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Obtain California seller's permit, workers' compensation insurance, and EDD employer registration. What to say: Register for a seller's permit at onlineservices.cdtfa.ca.gov (free, often same-day). CDTFA may request a security deposit depending on projected sales. Register as an employer with EDD at edd.ca.gov/Payroll_Taxes within 15 days of paying wages; your payroll provider needs the EDD account number before the first pay run. Purchase workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Compensation Insurance Fund (required from the first employee, even part-time); several city permits ask for proof of coverage. Set up organics (green bin) collection with your hauler to comply with SB 1383 before opening.

What to say: Register for a seller's permit at onlineservices.cdtfa.ca.gov (free, often same-day). CDTFA may request a security deposit depending on business type and projected taxable sales. Register as an employer with EDD at edd.ca.gov/Payroll_Taxes within 15 days of paying more than $100 in wages in a quarter; your payroll provider needs the EDD account number before the first pay run. Purchase workers' compensation insurance from a licensed carrier or State Compensation Insurance Fund (required from the first employee, even part-time); several city permits ask for proof of coverage. Set up organics (green bin) collection with your hauler to comply with SB 1383 before opening.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Certify a food safety manager and enroll employees in food handler card and RBS training (if alcohol is added later). What to say: At least one owner or employee must pass an ANSI-accredited food safety certification exam (ServSafe, Prometric, NRFSP, or 360training) within 60 days of opening; the certificate ($100–$250, valid 5 years) is required at the DPH pre-opening inspection. Every employee who handles food must obtain a California Food Handler Card ($7–$15, 2-hour online course, valid 3 years) within 30 days of hire. If you add alcohol service later, every server and manager must complete RBS training within 60 days of hire ($3 registration + $10–$25 course); ABC inspects for the certification list.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Apply for health permit to operate after final building and fire inspections. What to say: Submit the permit to operate application online at sfdph.org/dph/EH/Food at least one month before opening, with your BAN, Location ID (LIN), EIN, and proof that a certified food safety manager is on staff. The $470 application fee (FY 2026–27) includes the initial inspection; the annual license fee for restaurants is $0 for 2026–28. Schedule the final health inspection after DBI and SFFD sign off; failed inspections (missing hand sinks, unsealed surfaces, no hot water) push openings by 2–3 weeks, so walk the space against the DPH checklist a week before. The permit is issued only after the final inspection passes; you cannot serve the public before it is issued.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 14 to 120 days. Estimated government cost: $470 to $1,000. Notes: The day range (14–120 days) and government cost range ($470–$1,000) cover the health permit to operate and building permit with change of use, the two approvals in the entitlement path, measured from application to approval when they are granted. The health permit alone is 14–45 days and $470–$1,000; the building permit is 14–120 days and $800–$15,000 depending on construction valuation. These figures assume the zoning status becomes 'allowed' after the two missing inputs (formula retail status and floor area) are confirmed. If either input triggers a Conditional Use Authorization hearing, add 120–300 days and $3,100–$15,000 for the CUA, and the overall timeline becomes 134–420 days. The cost range does not include construction, architect fees, equipment, or non-government expenses such as workers' compensation insurance premiums. The day count is the time to approval, not to denial or withdrawal; no figures are given for those outcomes because the concept is not proposed for denial.
